title: Rama asks the trees
hookLine: the hero weeps in the empty forest: God, living as a man, grieves
carry: avatar: god lived a human grief
tomorrow: who has waited years for Rama to walk up her path?

cards: Rama is running. He has chased the golden deer deep into the forest, killed it, and heard it shout in his own voice. Racing back through the trees, he meets Lakshmana coming toward him, alone, and his heart drops.

This is the prince who accepted exile in one sentence, who faced fourteen thousand warriors alone, whose face, Valmiki says, didn't change when he lost a kingdom. The brothers reach the clearing together.
The hut is there. Sita is not.

teach.b: What happens next doesn't flatter its hero. Rama runs from tree to tree, calling her name, asking the trees if they've seen her. He asks the deer, and in Valmiki's telling the deer all turn their heads and look south.
He weeps until he can barely stand. Then the grief turns into rage.
He tells Lakshmana he'll fill the sky with arrows and tear the worlds apart until the gods give her back.

It's the younger brother, usually the hothead, who calms him: you're the one who taught everyone patience, he says, in effect. Don't become the storm. Then they find Jatayu, and Rama holds the dying bird.

Why would a story about God on earth show him coming apart? On day thirty-six you met avatara: God coming down, born as one of us. Hindus who worship Rama as Vishnu's avatar don't read these tears as a flaw in the story.
Many read them as the point.

teach.h: AVATAR: GOD LIVES A HUMAN LIFE.
teach.b: He didn't wear a human life like a costume.

teach.h: GOD ON EARTH, AND HE WEEPS.
teach.b: He lived it, and a human life includes losing someone you love. Remember the morning his face didn't change at the news of exile. Losing a kingdom, he stayed still.
Losing Sita, he can't. And Lakshmana doesn't scold him. He stays beside him, and turns him back toward the search.

That's why many devotees bring God their grief without hiding it: the God they pray to has stood in an empty clearing calling a name. When you, or someone strong you love, comes apart, the tradition doesn't say be strong.
It says even Rama wept, and someone sat beside him.

how: Rama's lament in the forest is recited and sung in Ramayana readings, and Ramlila performances often stage it as an emotional scene; many devotees speak of Rama's grief as part of the full human life of Vishnu's avatar, and many Hindus say Rama's name in hard hours.

o: the steady hero coming apart in grief
Rama breaking his promise to stay in exile
Rama's army breaking through Lanka's walls

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: turned their heads and looked south
what Rama asks where she went
God born as one of us, living a full life

s: the Ramayana hides Rama's grief to keep him heroic
it shows him running tree to tree, weeping and raging.
Rama threatens to fill the sky with arrows
his grief turns to rage until Lakshmana talks him down.
it's Rama who calms Lakshmana down here
it's the other way around. Lakshmana calms Rama.

games.q: a classmate says: 'if Rama is God, his crying is fake. he already knew how it ends.' what fits today's teaching?
o: right, it's just acting for the audience.
for Hindus who see him as an avatar, he truly lived a human life, grief and all.
no Hindu thinks Rama is God, so it doesn't matter.
games.why: avatara means God coming down to live as one of us. many devotees read Rama's tears as real, and as the point.

practice: Think of a strong person in your life who is grieving, and sit beside them in your mind, the way Lakshmana sits beside Rama. Don't try to fix it.
If you pray, say Rama's name softly a few times, the way many Hindus do in hard hours: Ram, Ram. If you don't, just stay with them, unhurried. If a grief of your own comes up, let it sit there too.

wordCard.voice: Rama breaks. The hero, in the empty forest, asking the trees where she went. The poem doesn't hide it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: lament, weeping aloud; Rama's lament in the forest.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: avatar. God lived a human grief, and Lakshmana sat beside him. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda (Rama's search and lament; Lakshmana calms him, roughly sargas 60–66)
